chapter_title: Concerning the Garment of the Waters: how great is its Measure.
chapter_note: The chapter is wrapped in a biographical-hagiographic riverbank scene (Tigris, Shapur, disciples’ praise). The oldest teaching substrate emerges sharply in ¶6–¶10 as an impersonal cosmological mechanism: First Man’s assumption of the elements and the water-garment’s vast measure (seven rivers into the rulers’ mouths; binding of destructive powers; the Tigris as a negligible fraction). Several teaching paragraphs retain later dialogue/address intrusions ("apostle", "elect one", "I told you" / cross-reference to the Great Gospel), so they are treated as MIXED with those secondary accretions removed.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Biographical court-setting with King Shapur and the formulaic opener "Once again"—a classic hagiographic frame, not cosmological exposition.
Extended scene-setting narrative (month-name, city, flood detail). This functions as story-container for the later lesson; it does not map cosmos→cosmos.
Narrative continues with institutional markers ("leaders of his church") and the apostle/disciple staging—editorial frame around the teaching.

Dialogue-question embedded in the Tigris scene; although it asks about the water-garment, it is tightly anchored to the narrative present (Tigris/sea imagery) and presented as a disciple’s speech to the "apostle"—best read as framing prompt rather than substrate exposition.
Direct-address exhortation ("listen", "be astonished") introduced by dialogue attribution "Then the apostle says"—a didactic transition in the compilation frame.

paragraphs.core_text: [At] the time when the First Man assumed the elements, and stood [fi]rm against the first enmity that had come about in the darkness, he defied these great and powerful rulers. They are immeasurable, greater than the extent or size of thousands and ten thousands of parasangs. At the start, when he spread the fight against them, he gave them fire and wind; and afterwards he gave the garment of the waters to the rulers of death. So they, the rulers, drank in and consumed those waters. Many [waters] poured forth from the garment of waters [...] the rivers flow. The mouth of the rulers [...] those [...], the warriors of destruction [...] laboured and brought them forth.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed the cross-reference/citation-aside anchored to Mani’s book-tradition and audience address: “, [the way that I told] you in the Great Gospel.” This is later intra-corpus referencing rather than impersonal substrate mechanism.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Core mechanism (First Man, elements as weapons/garments, immeasurable rulers, hydraulic outflow) is systematic cosmology. The explicit self-reference to prior teaching in a named book (“Great Gospel”) and second-person address marks later editorial/bookish insertion.

paragraphs.core_text: There were seven (rivers), like the great river Tigris [that you] see, flowing in to the mouth of each one of them, as they shall not [...] to a single stomach, to their fill; because in turn the descent to its stomach shall burn them with its fire and heat. Those rulers were like the [...] of [...]; they were not emptied; rain and [...] their existent days.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Systematic numeric cosmology (“seven rivers”) describing a cosmic digestive/fire process within the rulers—cosmos→cosmos mapping and mechanism, not institutional application.

paragraphs.core_text: The measure of that river was expanded seven times, as they flow [...] of the body of the [...] waters [...] now.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed dialogue attribution and institutional address: “The apostle speaks to that elect one:”. Removed the ensuing exhortational marveling sequence (“Marvel at ... you marvel ... Marvel first ...”) as application/performative closure rather than impersonal measurement teaching.
paragraphs.temporal_note: The surviving line preserves a compact quantitative/measure teaching (expansion “seven times”) within the elemental-water system. “apostle”/“elect one” and repeated imperatives to marvel are later pedagogical overlay onto the teaching.

paragraphs.core_text: [...] is how great a struggle, since it has [...] these creatures of destruction, the mighty giants. Behold, they are entwined, bound, and [...] in every place. They are hidden, not revealed before the eyes of every flesh that exists on the land of death [...]. These rulers [...] revealed. The entire universe of flesh will be destroyed and dissolved [...]; all pass away [...]. They will be destroyed with their angry voice, which is mightier than the thunder.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Cosmic containment and eschatological dissolution described as process (binding, hiddenness, destruction of the flesh-universe). No institutional targeting; “Behold” is rhetorical but remains within cosmic architecture.

paragraphs.core_text: Now, as this small stream is reckoned [...] before the vastness of these waters of which I have recounted to you. For only one river from thousands of rivers of water, from the secrets that are not revealed, is the river Tigris upon the earth.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Comparative measure logic (one earthly river vs thousands of hidden rivers) serves the cosmological scale-teaching; despite the second-person “to you,” the mapping remains cosmos→cosmos (secret rivers/waters) with the Tigris as a minimal exemplar.

paragraphs.core_text: [...] the measure of the elements of the waters. [...] the stature of the Man who bore them. [...] how great is that god, active in power, the one whom these waters [...] than the stature of the First Man who [assumed] this garment of such size; and how much was made.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed the imperative/exhortational address that frames the content: “See [...] and be amazed ... Marvel ... And understand ...” These are homiletic cues rather than substrate exposition.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Underlying content is a scale-comparison within the elemental/First Man system (measure of waters; the bearer’s stature). The surrounding direct-address marveling is a later sermonic pedagogy layered onto the substrate.
Formal closing praise/thanks by disciples (“We revere you, our master… opened our eyes”)—a standard compilational/hagiographic closure.
